notes.body:
The word "likewise" is doing quiet but important legal work here. It points backward — not to anything named in this passage yet, but to a category already established in the tradition: the martyr (شهيد), the one who dies in the cause of Allah on the field of battle. The ruling that a martyr is not washed before burial is one of the foundational distinctions in Islamic funerary law, and it is the silent benchmark against which the wounded man is being measured.

**What defines the martyr's exemption from ritual washing (غسل) is precisely that he was not lifted from the place where he fell.** The battlefield soil, the blood, the position in which he met Allah — all of this is left undisturbed, because that condition is itself considered a form of sacred purity. The text then applies that same criterion to the wounded man — he was not moved, he lived on, he spoke, and when death came, he was still where he had fallen — and folds him into the same protected category.

The passage confirms this when it notes that if the martyr was in a state of ritual impurity (جنابة), he is washed on account of the ritual impurity — the exception only makes sense if the default rule is that martyrs are not washed at all. Even the martyr's sacred exemption can be overridden — but only by ritual impurity (جنابة). The wounded man who never left his place inherits that same dignity: buried in the condition in which Allah received him, the washing that ordinarily honours the dead is here withheld as an even deeper honour.
notes.anchor: he is likewise not washed, because he was not lifted from his place
notes.quote: he is likewise not washed, because he was not lifted from his place
etymology: شهيد (martyr, witness): from the root ش-ه-د, meaning to be present, to witness, to testify. The martyr is the ultimate witness — one who testifies with their life. The same root gives شَهَادَة, both testimony and the declaration of faith. Dying in Allah's cause makes one permanently, actively present in His sight.

جنابة (ritual impurity): from the root ج-ن-ب, meaning to be to the side, set apart, or at a distance. This state holds a person at the periphery of worship until purification is performed. The root also gives جَنْب (side) and جَانِب (beside) — the image of someone standing aside, waiting to be restored.

غسل (ritual washing): from the root غ-س-ل, meaning to wash or cleanse with flowing water. The root is direct: water moving over the body carries impurity away with it. It gives both the act غُسْل (the washing itself) and the substance غَسُول (water for washing), holding action and instrument in one family.

notes.body:
The phrase "the more excellent of them" compares the man in a state of ritual impurity (جنابة) against the other washers present — not against the deceased. The question settled here is whether جنابة disqualifies a person entirely when alternatives exist; the answer is no.

The quality being measured is **ritual fitness**: a compound of religious knowledge, familiarity with the washing procedure according to the sunnah, piety, and community standing. Someone who knows the order of the limbs, the number of washings, and how to manage the cloth over what must remain covered is more excellent as a washer than someone technically pure but ignorant of the rite. Ritual impurity is an impediment, but it does not erase qualifications — it is weighed against them.

The text builds a ranked set of cases:
- When no one else is available, the washer in جنابة proceeds regardless, doing تيمم first if the full bath would harm him.
- When others are present but the person in جنابة surpasses them in qualification, his washing remains permitted.
- When equally or more qualified washers are present and ritually pure, preference passes to them.

The Arabic word أفضل, which stands behind "more excellent," comes from a root meaning surplus — bounty that overflows its vessel. In jurisprudential writing, it marks **measurable superiority**: the kind that gives someone the better right to lead a rite.

notes.quote: if the man in janabah is the more excellent of them, his washing of the dead is permitted
etymology: جنابة (ritual impurity): from root ج-ن-ب, meaning to be at one's side, then by extension to be set apart or distant. A person in this state is estranged from ritual purity until the full bath is performed. The root captures the distance the condition creates between a person and sacred acts — a temporary separation, not a permanent one.

تيمم (dry ablution): from root ي-م-م, meaning to aim toward or to intend. Performing تيمم is a directed act — turning one's intention toward the earth as a purposeful substitute for water when water is absent or harmful. The root preserves the idea that purification is always a conscious reaching, even when the means must change.

أفضل (the more excellent): from root ف-ض-ل, meaning surplus or bounty that overflows its vessel. Something أفضل has more of a quality than what is merely sufficient — it surpasses by excess of virtue. In jurisprudential use, it identifies the person whose accumulated merit gives them the stronger right to perform or lead a sacred act.

notes.body:
The hanut (حنوط) is the aromatic mixture applied to the deceased before burial — a final gesture of reverence and care. Camphor (كافور) forms its required base, but additional perfumes may be added. Wars (ورس) and saffron (زعفران) are among those extras, though the sources **reserve them for women's hanut** and exclude them from a man's.

Wars (ورس) is a plant native to the highlands of Yemen. Its dried leaves and flowers are crushed into a striking yellow-orange powder, traded across the Arabian Peninsula as both a fabric dye and a body cosmetic. Both are **warm, pigmenting substances** long associated with feminine adornment.

The reason flows from a **single governing principle** — Maulana Ali (ع) stated it in his Four Hundred Counsels:

> وَلَا تُجَمِّرُوا مَوْتَاكُمْ وَلَا تَمَسُّوهُمْ بِالطِّيبِ اِلَّا بِالْكَافُورِ فَاِنَّ الْمَيِّتَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْمُحْرِمِ
>
> Do not perfume your dead with incense, and do not touch them with any fragrance except camphor, for the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage.

The deceased man is prepared as a محرم — one in إحرام. **Classical jurisprudence names wars and saffron** among the substances such a man must avoid. A woman faces no such restriction on these coloring substances, and that difference follows her into death — she receives in her hanut what she would be permitted as a living woman pilgrim.

Wars and saffron are not withheld from men out of frugality. They are withheld because **death is an entry into the sacred** — and the body is prepared as one already consecrated to Allah.

notes.quote: neither wars nor saffron is put into the hanut of men, while these are put into the hanut of women
etymology: ورس: from the root و-ر-س, whose verb وَرَسَ means to yield a yellow or golden-orange dye. The plant ورس is named for this single quality — it is literally the yellowing thing. Classical lexicographers treat it as either a pure Arabic word of Yemeni origin or a loanword from a South Arabian language carried north along the trade routes.

حنوط: from the root ح-ن-ط, whose verb حَنَّطَ means to treat a body with aromatic spices — to prepare and embalm it for burial. The حنوط is the substance used in that act. The root carries a sense of careful readying: anointing and preserving something at the very threshold between this world and what lies beyond.

محرم: from the root ح-ر-م, meaning to forbid or to make sacred and inviolable. This root yields حَرَام (the forbidden), الحَرَم (the sacred sanctuary), and إحرام (the state of consecration). A محرم is one for whom certain things are now forbidden — and that very act of forbidding is what makes the person sacred, as a sanctuary is sacred.

زعفران: the word's origin is debated — some scholars link it to an Arabic root for golden-yellow color; others see it as a borrowing from Persian, where زَر means gold. The word likely traveled with the spice along the trade routes, carrying in its name the color that defined it: crimson threads that steep into warm, radiant gold.

notes.body:
The equivalence between the dead and the state of ritual consecration (إحرام) is not a loose metaphor — it rests on a precise doctrinal insight about what death actually is. إحرام marks the moment a pilgrim crosses a threshold: they shed worldly dress, renounce fragrance and pleasure, and enter a condition entirely consecrated to Allah. **Death is precisely that same crossing**, only final and irreversible — the soul has left the domain of the world (دنيا) and can no longer hold any claim on its pleasures.

This is why Maulana Ali's ruling in the Four Hundred Counsels carries the weight it does. He does not say the dead merely resemble the pilgrim in some poetic sense — he uses the word station (مَنْزِلَة), the actual rank a person occupies. **The dead person has arrived at the rank of the consecrated pilgrim**, and the practical consequences follow directly: no fragrance may touch the body except camphor (كافور), and the shroud (كفن) is a simple unwoven white cloth that echoes the إحرام garment.

Camphor (كافور) is the one permitted exception, and **the permission is itself a confirmation of the rule**. It is cool and preserving rather than pleasurable, and in the Quran it names a spring among the blessings awaiting the righteous:

إِنَّ الْأَبْرَارَ يَشْرَبُونَ مِن كَأْسٍ كَانَ مِزَاجُهَا كَافُورًا
The righteous drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor.
Al-Insan 76:5

Camphor belongs, symbolically, to the world the dead are approaching — and that is exactly why it may be used while worldly fragrances may not.

As for whether this status applies to all the dead: Maulana Ali uses the definite الميت, meaning **the dead person as a recognized category**, not as a named exception. The text does identify one special case — a person who dies while in actual إحرام during pilgrimage carries an additional restriction, because their personal consecration still has active days running, and so the head and face may not be covered. But the إحرام-like station, and the prohibition on fragrance, holds for every deceased person regardless of the circumstances of their death.
notes.anchor: the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage
notes.quote: the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage
etymology: إحرام (ritual consecration): from the root ح-ر-م, to forbid or to make sacred. The same root yields حَرَام (the forbidden), حَرَم (the sacred precinct), and مُحْرِم (the consecrated person). The act of entering إحرام — أَحْرَمَ — literally means he made himself forbidden to the world. The word captures a single movement: a person steps out of ordinary life and into divine custody.

مَنْزِلَة (station): from the root ن-ز-ل, to descend or to alight. A مَنْزِلَة is the place where someone has come to rest — a rank, a stage, a resting point on a journey. When Maulana Ali says the dead person occupies the مَنْزِلَة of the consecrated pilgrim, he means the dead has alighted at that exact ritual station, not merely approached it.

الميت (the dead person): from the root م-و-ت, meaning death and cessation of life. The form مَيِّت is an intensive adjective — not merely dead but thoroughly, completely so. The definite article الـ makes الميت a recognized category of person with established ritual standing, not simply a body awaiting disposal.

كافور (camphor): an ancient loanword in Arabic, tracing back through Persian and Sanskrit origins. In Arabic use, its association with كَفَرَ — to cover and conceal — places it in the register of preservation. Its Quranic appearance in Al-Insan links it to the blessings of the next world, setting it apart from the worldly fragrances that إحرام forbids.
